etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle French sincere, from Latin sincerus (“genuine”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- + *ḱer- (“grow”), from which also Ceres (“goddess of harvest”) from which English cereal.

Unrelated to sine (“without”) + cera (“wax”) (folk etymology); see Wikipedia page.

definitions.definition: Genuine; meaning what one says or does; heartfelt.

quote.citation: 1837, Thomas Carlyle, chapter III, in The French Revolution: A History […], volume II (The Constitution), London: Chapman and Hall, →OCLC, book I (The Feast of Pikes), page 19:
quote.text: Tumid blustering, with more or less of sincerity, which need not be entirely sincere, yet the sincerer the better, is like to go far.

quote.citation: 1967 June, Drake Maynard, If, volume 17, number 6, page 160:
quote.text: My sincerest apologies to Brother Ron Smith in the December ish.

quote.citation: 2003, “The Outsider”, performed by A Perfect Circle:
quote.text: If you choose to pull the trigger, should your drama prove sincereDo it somewhere far away from here

quote.citation: 1996, Macy Nulman, The Encyclopedia of Jewish Prayer, page 161:
quote.text: The message that through sincere teshuvah and resolution, light and gladness can be achieved by all, is most fitting for the opening of the Yom Kippur service.
